questions.passage: In the early days of commercial aviation, the captain's authority in the cockpit was rarely questioned. Investigations of several accidents in the 1970s, however, found that other crew members had noticed problems but hesitated to speak up. In response, airlines developed training known as Crew Resource Management (CRM), which teaches every crew member to share observations, state concerns clearly, and work through decisions together. Today the approach has spread beyond aviation to fields such as surgery and firefighting.

questions.passage: Pilots often say that hot, high, and humid conditions are an airplane's enemy. As air warms, rises in elevation, or holds more moisture, it becomes less dense. Thinner air gives the wings less to push against, so the airplane needs a longer runway to reach takeoff speed, and the engine and propeller produce less power. On a summer afternoon at a mountain airport, density altitude can be thousands of feet higher than the field's actual elevation, and a takeoff that is routine on a cool morning may become dangerous.

questions.passage: Many students cut back on sleep before a big exam so they can study longer. Research on memory suggests this trade is often a poor one. During sleep, especially deep sleep early in the night, the brain replays and strengthens information learned during the day, moving it into longer-lasting memory. People who sleep after learning a list of words or a new skill usually remember it better the next day than people who stay awake for the same number of hours. Sleep loss also weakens attention, so a tired student may read the same page several times without absorbing it. An extra hour of study can be worth less than the hour of sleep it replaces.
